e.t: This word means “marketplace” or “marketplaces,” referring to a public place where people gathered and goods were bought or sold. It is a noun used for such locations, whether one marketplace or more than one. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 11 times, including passages describing public settings in the towns and cities of Jesus’ ministry and in Acts. Its basic meaning remains the physical marketplace; the surrounding verse determines what people are doing there or why the place is mentioned.

This word means “praise,” an expression of honor, approval, or commendation. It refers to words or an expression that speaks well of someone and recognizes their worth. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Hebrews 13:15. Its single occurrence makes it a focused term rather than a frequently repeated word, but its central meaning remains clear: praise is an outward expression of honor offered to the one being praised.

This word refers to an audience room or hall—a place where people gather to hear a speaker or appear before an official. It is a noun describing the setting rather than the people assembled there. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs only once, in Acts 25:23. The word therefore identifies a formal public venue, while the surrounding verse is needed to explain the specific event taking place in that hall.

This word describes someone who cannot rightly be charged with wrongdoing—someone “blameless” and “irreproachable.” It points to a life that withstands examination without a valid accusation, rather than claiming that the person has never made a mistake. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs five times, including descriptions of believers and of those considered for responsible service in the church. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This word means “severity” or “sternness”—a strict, uncompromising quality rather than gentleness or softness. It describes the serious firmness with which something is carried out or maintained. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both within one verse in Romans, and its English rendering there is “severity.” The related idea can therefore point to a demanding or severe manner, but the surrounding verse is needed to explain exactly what is severe and how the word functions in that passage.

This word describes someone or something that is competent and thorough—properly equipped, complete, and able to fulfill its intended purpose. It points to adequacy and readiness rather than merely appearing finished. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Timothy 3:17. There it describes the person shaped by Scripture, emphasizing that Scripture equips that person for every good work. The word’s central sense is therefore being fully prepared and capable for the task required.

This word describes something that is spotless—free from a mark, blemish, or stain. It can be used of a person or thing viewed as clean and without fault in the New Testament’s wording. The word occurs four times in the Greek New Testament, appearing in 1 Timothy, James, 1 Peter, and 2 Peter. Its precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains being without spot.

Achaicus is a personal name referring to a man mentioned in the Greek New Testament. It is a name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or spiritual idea. This name occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in 1 Corinthians 16:17. The name itself identifies the person, while the surrounding verse and passage provide the details of his role and circumstances. Its English rendering is consistently “Achaicus.”

Bartimaeus is a personal name, referring to a particular man rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek New Testament, it appears once, in Mark 10:46, and is rendered as “Bartimaeus.” Because names identify people, the word’s basic meaning is its identifying name; the surrounding verse and passage are needed to explain what happens to this man or why he is mentioned there. This entry therefore identifies a person’s name rather than providing a broader vocabulary meaning.

This word means a “pit,” referring to a depression or opening in the ground. It is a noun used for a physical place into which something or someone could fall. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, all in Matthew and Luke. Its repeated use in sayings about falling or being led into danger keeps the central picture concrete: a pit is a hazardous place below ground that can trap or harm someone. The surrounding verse determines the specific application in each occurrence.

This word means “slowness,” describing a lack of speed or a delay in action. It appears once in the Greek New Testament, at 2 Peter 3:9. The word itself names the quality of being slow, while the surrounding sentence determines what is slow and how that slowness relates to the passage. Its meaning is therefore straightforward but context-dependent: it points to delayed movement, action, or response rather than quickness.

e.t: This word means “to deliver a public address” or “to give a speech.” It describes spoken communication directed to an audience, rather than a private remark or brief comment. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 12:21. The word identifies the act of making a public address, while the surrounding passage determines the occasion, purpose, and significance of that speech.

This word means “to disunite” or “to turn,” describing an action that separates rather than joins. It functions as a verb, expressing the act of dividing or turning people or things apart. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, at Matthew 10:35. The precise force of “to turn” in that verse depends on its surrounding passage, but the word’s basic idea is separation or a decisive turning.

Pregnant means carrying a child in the womb. In the Greek New Testament, this word occurs once, in Luke 2:5, and gives a direct physical description of pregnancy. It refers to the state of expecting a baby, rather than naming an action, feeling, or spiritual quality. Its basic meaning is clear; the surrounding verse supplies the particular details of how it is used there.

e.t: This word means “to supply” or “to support,” describing the provision of what is needed so that someone or something can continue, grow, or become fully equipped. It can refer to God supplying what people need, or to people supplying what contributes to spiritual progress. The word occurs five times in the Greek New Testament, including passages about provision, growth, and entrance into Christ’s everlasting kingdom. Its precise emphasis in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This word means “acceptable,” describing something regarded as suitable or welcome. It can describe what is received favorably in relation to God or others, while the surrounding verse determines exactly what is being called acceptable. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs five times across Romans, 2 Corinthians, and 1 Peter. Its central idea remains simple: something meets the relevant standard and is received as acceptable.

This word refers to an Ephesian or to the Ephesians, the people identified with Ephesus. It functions as a people-name or regional designation rather than describing an action, quality, or spiritual condition. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs five times, all in Acts, where it identifies people connected with Ephesus. The singular sense is “Ephesian,” while the plural sense is “Ephesians.”

This word means “day” or “days”. It refers to a period of time identified as a day, or to multiple such periods. In the Greek New Testament, it is used broadly—389 times—so it can mark ordinary time without itself supplying the larger meaning of a passage. The singular and plural renderings simply reflect whether one day or more than one is meant. Its range extends throughout the New Testament, from Matthew through Revelation. The surrounding words determine the specific time being discussed.

This word means “as” or “just as,” linking one statement, action, or condition with another for comparison or correspondence. It helps show that something happens in a similar way, according to a matching pattern, or in relation to what has already been said. It is a common connecting word in the Greek New Testament, occurring 182 times. Its exact force—whether simple comparison, resemblance, or correspondence—depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central function is to connect related ideas by saying that one is like or in agreement with another.

e.t: This word means “to become corroded” or “to corrode,” describing material that is eaten away, damaged, or weakened through corrosion. It is a verb expressing an action or resulting condition rather than naming an object. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in James 5:3. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the central idea remains decay caused by corrosion. e.t: This word means “to divine” or “to fortune-tell”—to seek or provide knowledge through divination rather than ordinary observation. It is a verb describing the act of practicing this kind of supernatural prediction. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 16:16. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself identifies the practice of fortune-telling or divination, not simply making a wise guess or offering an ordinary prediction.

This Greek New Testament verb means “to flog” or “to whip,” describing the act of striking someone repeatedly with a whip or similar instrument. It is an action word rather than a title, quality, or object. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in Acts 22:25. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is the infliction of flogging or whipping. [p03:word:greek-nt:G3147:identity] [p01:word:greek-nt:G3147:reference:0]

This word means “be gentle” or “to deal gently.” It describes treating someone with mildness and restraint rather than harshness. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Hebrews 5:2. As a verb, it expresses gentle action toward another person. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself centers on responding with gentleness, especially when dealing with human weakness or failure.

Uzziah is a personal name, referring to a particular man rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek New Testament, it appears twice, both times in Matthew 1:8–9, and is rendered “Uzziah.” Its role is therefore that of a person’s name within the genealogy recorded in Matthew. The precise significance of mentioning him belongs to that genealogy’s surrounding context, but the word itself identifies Uzziah.

e.t: This word means “to refuse” or “to excuse,” describing the act of declining something or giving a reason for not accepting it. Its use can refer to refusing a request, turning away from an invitation, or offering an excuse. It occurs 12 times in the Greek New Testament, with “refuse” being the predominant English rendering. The surrounding passage determines whether the emphasis is on rejection itself or on the explanation given for declining.

This word means “by the sea” or “seaside,” describing something located beside the sea. It functions as a concise place-related description rather than naming a person, object, or action. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Luke 6:17. Its basic sense is straightforward: it identifies a location near the sea. The surrounding verse determines what person or group is being associated with that location, but the word itself contributes the idea of being at or near the seaside.

This word means “to premeditate” or “to worry beforehand.” It describes thinking about something in advance, especially by preparing one’s thoughts before the moment arrives. As a verb, it points to prior mental consideration rather than action occurring immediately. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Luke 21:14. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the act of considering or being concerned about something ahead of time.

“Poverty” refers to a condition of lacking material resources or living with very little. This Greek New Testament noun names an economic condition rather than an action, person, or feeling. It occurs three times in the Greek New Testament, in two passages in 2 Corinthians and one in Revelation, and each occurrence is rendered “poverty.” The word therefore keeps a consistent basic sense across its uses: real material need or deprivation. Its precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself points to poverty plainly.

This word describes something characterized by fire or by a fiery-red appearance. It can identify a vivid color or quality that resembles flames, emphasizing intensity and brightness rather than merely naming ordinary redness. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, so its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and imagery. Its recorded rendering is “fiery,” while “fiery red” also expresses the word’s meaning. [p03:word:greek-nt:G4447:identity] [p01:word:greek-nt:G4447:reference:0]

e.t: This verb means “to be darkened” or “to darken,” describing the loss or removal of light. It can refer to something becoming dark or being made dark. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, in Ephesians and Revelation, and its exact force depends on what is being described in each passage. The word can therefore express either a darkened condition or the action that produces darkness, while keeping the central idea of becoming deprived of light.

This word means “united,” describing people or things joined together rather than remaining separate. It expresses a shared connection or likeness, and its precise force in a sentence depends on what is being joined. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Romans 6:5. The word’s basic sense points to participation in a common union, making it suitable for describing close association or being joined with another. Its English rendering is “united.”

e.t: This word means to understand—to grasp the meaning of something so that it is recognized clearly. It describes inward comprehension, not merely hearing words. In the Greek New Testament, it appears 26 times, often in contexts where people are expected to perceive the meaning of teaching, words, or events. The word is rendered “understand” in the English evidence and can describe either a person’s act of comprehending or the result of that comprehension.

This word means “self-discipline,” describing the inward restraint and sound control that enable a person to act rightly rather than be ruled by fear or impulse. It appears once in the Greek New Testament, at 2 Timothy 1:7. As a normal word meaning self-discipline, it points to a settled capacity for responsible, controlled conduct. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This word means “three hundred,” expressing a specific quantity or number. It is a numerical term rather than a description of a person, action, or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, in Mark 14:5 and John 12:5. Its basic meaning remains the same wherever it appears; the surrounding sentence identifies what is being counted or valued. The word itself communicates the amount, while the verse context supplies its particular significance.

This word means “manifestation”: something made evident or openly shown. It points to the making visible or recognizable of something that might otherwise remain unseen. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs two times, in 1 Corinthians 12:7 and 2 Corinthians 4:2, and is rendered “manifestation” in both passages. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is clear: a revealing or showing forth that makes something known.

This word means a “piece” or “piece of bread,” referring to a portion separated from a loaf or other bread. It is used four times in the Greek New Testament, all within three verses in John 13. The wording points to an individual piece rather than bread in general. Its normal meaning is therefore concrete and specific: a portion of bread that can be taken, given, or eaten. The exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding passage and sentence.
